items.excerpt: Nov. 1, 2026, 6:00 PM EST By Mark Hodge and Kayla Hayempour Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday, a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race that could determine which party controls the Senate. The congresswoman’s announcement marks a whirlwind turnabout from just days ago, amid a dispute with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign over an outside ad that Stevens said was antisemitic. NBC News reported Saturday that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to no longer attend campaign events. “Hey, Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video. “And he’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” she said. ## Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling steep Democratic advantage Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark across his two terms in the NBC News poll. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). But it’s not all good news for Democrats: The poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party. ## Federal judge dismisses Trump attempt to interfere in Alaska Senate race Alaska's U.S. Senate candidates: Mary Peltola; Dan J. Sul ... Sullivan. Bloomberg; AP; Getty A federal judge in Alaska on Sunday dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit seeking to separate and preserve certain ballots in the state’s upcoming Senate election, where GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola. In the last week, Peltola’s campaign has faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported the campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate — Dan J. Sullivan — to run for the Senate with the same name as the incumbent senator. Citing potential voter confusion, the Trump administration sought to separate and preserve ballots with votes for Dan J. Sullivan, arguing that if the incumbent loses, it may be because people voted for the other Sullivan by mistake. In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason voiced concerns about voters’ right to a secret ballot. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., declined to say whether he would accept the results of the Alaska Senate race if Peltola wins. Asked on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether he would accept the results if Peltola is certified to have won the Senate seat, Scott did not directly answer the question. “Dan Sullivan is going to win, Kristen,” he told moderator Kristen Welker. “You know that, and that’s the only thing I’m going to tell you, because it’s the truth.” ... ## Stores looted in German riots as Gen Z activists protest living costs, military service ... Rioters looted stores and set fire to barricades in Frankfurt on Saturday as demonstrations across Germany called for lower living costs and better education. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets in more than 30 cities, including Berlin and Frankfurt, in protests organized by the campaign group Gen Z Regelt, or Gen Z Takes Charge. France, Italy, Serbia and Spain have seen protests against the cost of living, among other causes. As the demonstrations began Saturday afternoon in Paris, protesters were pictured holding a banner that read: “We do not need tear gas for our future to be blurry.” ... ## Golden State Valkyries defeat Atlanta Dream for first WNBA title ... In only their second season in existence, the Golden State Valkyries are WNBA champions. The Valkyries won their first title on Saturday, defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history. Forward Gabby Williams led with 30 points and was named MVP. Williams scored just two points in the first half, but rallied with 28 in the second, a record for the most points scored in a half in the WNBA postseason. Teammate Kiah Stokes led rebounds at 13. “This is just incredible,” Stokes said of her fourth championship title. “But just my teammates, they’re amazing. The love that we feel is just incredible. I mean, this one just might be as good as my first.” ... - A Learjet 60 jet heading for the Bahamas crashed in Florida Sunday afternoon, killing all nine people on board, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

items.title: Strong growth and inflation paints mixed picture of economy days before midterm elections | | midfloridanewspapers.com
items.excerpt: - By CHRISTOPHER RUGABER AP Economics Writer ... - Nov 1, 2026 - 17 hrs ago WASHINGTON — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country’s economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue. Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains. Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years. How long can this economic growth continue? Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans’ ability to keep up. Thursday’s data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier. “High energy prices are chipping away at purchasing power,” Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote. “Real income failed to grow for a second consecutive month, while the saving rate continued to decline. Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters.” Inflation worsens Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May. Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of the energy sector. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched. The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $4.23 on Thursday, 39% more than it cost a year ago. Diesel prices have risen much faster. While most consumers don’t buy diesel, it has an outsized impact on inflation because it is used in industrial sectors and shipping. “The inflation outlook has become more concerning,” Bushmeneva said. “Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening.” Polls show that rising inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks for his handling of rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. From August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month. Will rising inflation raise borrowing costs? The new economic growth and inflation numbers arrive a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combating inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is now much more likely to raise its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy. “If the Federal Reserve is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending, historically low jobless claims, stratospheric private non-residential investment, and sizzling inflation data,” Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax advisory firm, wrote. Thursday’s inflation data come from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers’ shopping habits.

items.title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose in September as third-quarter GDP beats expectations | The New York Ledger
items.excerpt: November 1, 2026 in News The Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge rose further away from the central bank’s target in September as consumers face price pressures. The Commerce Department on Thursday reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index rose 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and was up 3.6% from a year ago. Both figures were in line with the expectations of economists polled by LSEG. Core PCE, which excludes volatile measurements of food and energy prices, was up 0.3% on a monthly basis and 3.1% year over year. Those figures were both in line with economists’ expectations. FEDERAL RESERVE MAKES INTEREST RATE DECISION AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Federal Reserve policymakers are focused on the PCE headline figure as they try to bring inflation back to their long-run target of 2%, though they view core data as a better indicator of inflation. Compared with August’s readings, headline PCE ticked up from 3.4% to 3.6%, while core PCE rose from 3% to 3.1%. Goods prices were up 3.9% year over year, while services prices increased 3.5% from a year ago in September. The personal savings rate as a percentage of disposable personal income was 3.8%, down from 4% in August. Over the last two years, the savings rate has declined from a peak of 6.2% in April 2025 and from 5.6% in January 2026. While inflation moved further away from the Fed’s 2% target, the Commerce Department also released the advance estimate for third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP), which grew more than expected. The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated that third-quarter GDP was 3.4%, above the 3.2% estimate of economists polled by LSEG. The BEA will release two subsequent revisions of the third-quarter GDP data. ... The market continues to expect the Fed to hike interest rates by 25 basis points in December, which would bring the federal funds rate to a range of 4% to 4.25% once implemented. The CME FedWatch tool shows a 79.6% probability the Fed will hike by 25 basis points in December, down slightly from 84.2% yesterday but higher than the 73.3% probability a week ago.

items.excerpt: After consumer price index inflation hit a 40-year high of 9.1 per cent in the summer of 2022, it has gradually eased and hit an annual rate of 2.4 per cent in February. Then, it took off again. Mr. Trump’s tariffs have put upward pressure on inflation, but it’s the U.S.’s months-long war with Iran – resulting in much higher gas prices – that’s played an outsized role in the upswing. In September, the most recent month of data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, annual CPI growth hit 3.7 per cent. In response, the Fed raised benchmark interest rates in September for the first time since 2023 to a range of 3.75 to 4 per cent, despite Mr. Trump’s demands to slash borrowing costs. Economists widely expect more rate hikes in the coming months. ... ## Inflation is (once again) outpacing wages For six consecutive months, growth in average hourly wages has not kept up with rising prices. Americans’ purchasing power is on the decline, much like during the inflationary wave of a few years ago. In September, the average hourly wage grew 3 per cent year over year, below the rate of inflation at 3.7 per cent. Leading into the last presidential election in 2024 and during the early months of Mr. Trump’s second term, average wages were growing at a comfortably quicker pace than consumer prices. However, the sudden spike in inflation in March after the start of the U.S.-Iran war has quickly flipped the switch. Crude oil benchmarks remain at, or in excess of, US$100 a barrel, putting upward pressure on inflation. Meanwhile, wage growth has cooled from rates above 4 per cent. ... ## Gas prices are near all-time highs Rising fuel and gasoline prices have been the biggest contributor to accelerating inflation. In September, more than half of the monthly increase in CPI was due to gas prices, which rose 9.1 per cent. A voter survey by The New York Times reported that more than 40 per cent of Republicans disapprove of how Trump has handled gas prices. Mr. Trump had promised to lower gas prices for American households in 2024, but military action in Iran is achieving just the opposite, leading to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz through which one-quarter of the global crude usually travelled. Since the beginning of the conflict in February, gas prices have increased by more than 45 per cent, from a national average of US$3.1 per gallon in February to US$4.5 per gallon in September. Diesel prices in the U.S. have increased by more than 71 per cent, averaging over US$6 per gallon. ... In the past year, 44 per cent of Americans said they had trouble paying for at least one basic necessity, with 20 per cent stating they needed a food bank or food pantry, according to a study conducted this fall by the Pew Research Center. ... While grocery prices have only increased by about 3 per cent since the beginning of Mr. Trump’s second term in January, 2025, the average price of groceries has increased 33 per cent since the end of 2019 – becoming a major pain in the wallets of many Americans. Feeding America’s report found nearly half of those experiencing food insecurity had incomes too high to qualify for social support programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. items.title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling ...
items.excerpt: Nov. 1, 2026, 9:00 AM EST By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security. “Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now. Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years. Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election. ... It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular. Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties.

items.title: Movie News: 1st November 2026
items.excerpt: November 1, 2026 by bobwp ### Patrick Stewart’s final role, Cate Blanchett in Tokyo, Jailer 2 closes in on ₹800 crore & Nollywood’s ₦400 million October. Morning, all. A new month, and Sunday means our weekly lap of the world’s other film industries, but first, more on the loss of Sir Patrick Stewart. I’ll cover the confirmed weekend box office numbers in tomorrow’s post. Patrick Stewart’s farewell performance: Marvel Studios has confirmed that Avengers: Doomsday, which opens on 18 December, will be Sir Patrick Stewart’s final onscreen performance, which ends a 26-year run as Professor Xavier. It means he won’t appear in the already-filmed content for Avengers: Secret Wars. He appears opposite Sir Ian McKellen’s Magneto, and the pair have already appeared together in the trailers. McKellen’s tribute, in which he said Stewart wore his heart on his sleeve and was a man to rely on, to admire and, in his case, to love, ended by noting that Stewart’s farewell performance in Avengers: Doomsday is yet to be seen. McKellen recalled that when Stewart first told him about a Star Trek offer, he urged him to think of his stage career, which is advice that Stewart, happily for the rest of us, ignored. McKellen also officiated at Stewart’s 2013 wedding. Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine opposite Stewart’s Professor X, called him one of the greats of stage and screen, and Rebecca Romijn thanked him as a fellow mutant and a fellow member of Starfleet. The Far East: Cate Blanchett in Tokyo: At the Tokyo International Film Festival on Friday, the first five short films made through Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund were screened, with Blanchett joined for a Q&A by the fund’s directors Shahrbanoo Sadat and Mohammad Rasoulof, and with help from Perfect Days actor Kōji Yakusho. Sadat’s feature No Good Men was also at the London Film Festival this month. The festival runs until 4 November. Tamil cinema: Jailer 2 closes in on ₹800 crore: Rajinikanth’s Jailer 2 stands at ₹776.95 crore (about $81 million) worldwide and ₹435.4 crore net (about $45 million) in India after 16 days, according to Sacnilk, and it’s closing in on the ₹800 crore milestone. Its ₹509.45 crore gross in India is within ₹10 crore of the all-time Tamil record in India, held by 2.0. I’ll bring you the full third-weekend numbers tomorrow. Nollywood’s ₦400 million October: In Nigeria, faith-based hit Agbara Nla: The Return topped the chart for a fourth weekend with ₦32.8 million (about $25,000) from 5,477 admissions over 23–25 October, taking it to ₦408.3 million (about $307,000), which makes it the first October release ever to pass ₦400 million. By Thursday its total had reached ₦422.7 million (about $318,000). Among the new releases, the campus drama Tele x Zikora, directed by Adenike Adebayo-Esho, had the biggest opening with ₦26.9 million (about $20,000), while Clayface opened fourth with ₦16.8 million (about $13,000). Fusion Intelligence expects 2026 to pass the whole of 2025’s Nigerian box office total early this month, helped by higher ticket prices. Birthdays: Toni Collette, star of The Sixth Sense and Hereditary, turns 54 today, and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan of Devdas turns 53. Also celebrating is Rob Riggle (56), who stars in Christmas at the Kringles, which opened in US cinemas on Friday.

items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 1, 2026 - Nov 1, 2026 Updated 1 hr ago Director calls Broadway revival of ‘In the Heights’ at NY City Center a ‘balm for these times’ NEW YORK (AP) — David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater. The show, running for three weeks at New York City Center, features a new cast of Latino artists. Mendizábal emphasizes the importance of showcasing Latino communities, especially now. Miranda, who starred in the original production, reflects on the musical's enduring relevance. The revival comes amid immigration tensions, highlighting themes of gentrification and community. New and old cast members say the musical remains a celebration of the Latino immigrant experience, with its messages resonating strongly today. Heidi Klum reveals Halloween costume as her iconic party marks 25 years Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for Halloween. Klum unveiled her costume Saturday as her iconic costume party marked 25 years in New York. Klum was unrecognizable with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits. The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume. Houdini’s centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Houdini, a century after his death, continues to captivate. A rare essay by the escape artist has been published, shedding light on his early influences. A recent book revisits questions about the cause and date of his death. Houdini, born Erik Weisz, became an international celebrity known for his escape acts. His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated, with new theories challenging the official cause. Centennial events this weekend include a "Grand Houdini Centenarium" in Budapest, an auction in Hollywood, and seances in Chicago and Maryland. Despite the intrigue, experts say his legacy endures through his remarkable life. Scott Clifton and Tamara Tunie earn lead acting Daytime Emmys. 'General Hospital' wins again LOS ANGELES (AP) — Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” have won lead acting honors at the Daytime Emmy Awards. It's Clifton's second career trophy in the lead category. Tunie made her return to the soap opera genre after 17 years away. “General Hospital” won its record 19th trophy overall as outstanding drama and sixth in a row. Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category for her former Netflix show “With Love, Meghan.” Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. An introspective Kirk Franklin is no longer apologizing with 'I Am What I Am' album NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart.
